metaDescription: Five continuous feed garbage disposals under $100, from third horsepower to half horsepower units, compared on grind speed, mounting, cord and septic fit.
expertTake: The InSinkErator Badger 5 with cord is the best pick under $100 because it is half horsepower, comes with a power cord and uses the quick lock mount that most replacements need. The GE one third horsepower unit is the value pick for light cooking. Skip the cap entirely if you grind heavy scraps daily or want sound insulation, because those features start above it.
introParagraphs: A garbage disposal is a small electric motor spinning a flywheel with swivel impellers that push scraps against a shredder ring. The motor size sets how quickly the flywheel gets up to speed and how well it fights a jam, but the mounting system and cord decide whether you can install it yourself.

Prices move, and the $100 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. Units at this level use basic induction motors and little sound insulation, so the buying questions are motor strength, whether a cord is included, how it mounts to your existing sink flange, and whether your household cooks lightly or heavily.

products.name: InSinkErator Badger 5 Disposal With Cord, 1/2 HP
products.description:
The Badger 5 is the entry level half horsepower disposer from the brand with the most units in American kitchens. Its Dura-Drive induction motor spins the flywheel through a gear free path, so it starts quickly and tolerates the odd chicken bone better than a basic motor. The cord is included, which matters because many disposers ship bare and need a separate cord kit.

The Lift and Latch mount is the real convenience. A twist-on, twist-off quick lock lets you remove the unit from the mounting ring without unscrewing a flange, so replacement takes minutes if you already have a compatible ring. Compared with the Moen PRO, the Badger is a bit larger and heavier under the sink, but the mounting system is easier to live with when you swap it a decade from now.

Its limits are plain. It has only light sound insulation, it runs loud compared with the premium Evolution line, and a half horsepower motor will slow down on fibrous vegetables like celery. If you cook modestly and want a recognizable brand with parts support, it is the safe middle. Run cold water during use and for fifteen seconds after, and do not feed it grease or bulk coffee grounds.
products.bestFor: Households replacing an old InSinkErator who want a simple plug-in swap.
pros: 1/2 HP induction motor for everyday scraps
Lift and Latch quick lock mount

products.name: Moen Prep Series PRO GXP50C Compact Disposal With Cord
products.description:
The GXP50C is the compact choice. A half horsepower Vortex motor turns the flywheel at about 2,600 RPM, and the housing is shaped for tight sink cabinets where larger disposers collide with the trap. That compact shell makes it the easiest unit to fit under a shallow sink or beside a dishwasher hose.

It has a pre-installed power cord and a mounting system designed to swap in for most existing disposals, including other brands. That fit is useful if you do not know what mount ring your sink has. Compared with the Badger 5, the Moen is lighter and smaller, but it offers fewer sound-damping features and less brand reach for service parts.

The usual limits apply. A half horsepower motor is fine for everyday plates and peels, but it can bog down on dense or fibrous waste. Keep a hex key handy for freeing a jam from below and learn where the reset button sits. If cabinet space is your constraint, this is the better pick of the two half horsepower units.
products.bestFor: Tight cabinets where a full-size disposer will not clear the trap.
cons: Fewer service parts than the larger brands

products.name: Moen Prep Series 1/2 HP Disposal With Fast Track Mount
products.description:
The Prep Series is aimed at people who slice, dice and peel as part of basic meal prep and need a modest, dependable disposer. The Vortex motor spins at about 2,600 RPM, which is fast enough to pulverize everyday scraps into fine particles that clear the drain.

Fast Track technology is the install feature: the unit fits most existing assemblies, including other brands, and the power cord is pre-installed. Compared with the GXP50C, it uses a similar motor but is sold on the Fast Track mount rather than the compact housing. Compared with the Badger 5, the Moen promises faster mounting on unfamiliar flanges, but it has less brand reach in repair parts.

The weak point is endurance under heavy use. A budget induction motor will wear faster in a family that grinds scraps after every meal, and the unit has little sound insulation. For a couple or a small family it is a sensible replacement. Do not push fibrous waste, clean the grind chamber with ice and citrus, and avoid chemical drain cleaners.
products.bestFor: Small households replacing an unknown brand and wanting a quick fit.
pros: Fast Track mount fits many existing assemblies
cons: Not built for heavy daily grinding

products.name: GE Disposall 1/2 HP Continuous Feed Garbage Disposer
products.description:
The GE half horsepower disposer is the cheapest of the half horsepower units in this list. Its motor reaches over 2,600 RPM, a speed that the maker says suits grinding cooked meat, beans and seeds, and the box includes what a DIY installer needs.

Compared with the Badger 5, the GE offers similar horsepower for less, but it lacks the same quick lock mounting system and is less likely to match an existing InSinkErator ring. Compared with the one third horsepower GE below, it gives more headroom for the occasional tough scrap.

Expect a noisy motor and basic materials. A disposal at this level is an appliance you replace, not a heirloom. Keep the flywheel moving by running water, never put your hand inside and use the hex socket under the unit to free a jam.
products.bestFor: A cost-conscious DIY replacement with real half horsepower.
pros: Lowest cost among the 1/2 HP units
Suited to cooked meat, beans and seeds
cons: May not match an existing mount ring

products.name: GE Disposall 1/3 HP Continuous Feed Disposer
products.description:
The one third horsepower GE is the lowest tier in this guide. It spins at over 2,300 RPM and handles cooked pasta and fruit peels, which is what a single person or a couple who cooks lightly will mostly feed it.

Compared with the half horsepower GE, it is slower, jams sooner and is rated for lighter scraps. Compared with the Badger 5, it gives up the quick lock mount and the brand parts network. Its low cost is the main reason to buy it.

It is not a family workhorse. If you cook often or feed it dense scraps, buy a half horsepower unit instead. Run cold water, grind small portions and keep fibrous waste out of it.
products.bestFor: Single households and light cooks who want the cheapest working disposer.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Horsepower decides how fast the flywheel gets to speed and how well it fights a jam. The GE one third horsepower unit suits light scraps, while the Badger 5, Moen units and half horsepower GE cover most households. Larger motors mainly buy speed and jam resistance, not finer grinding, so do not pay for more than you cook. A common mistake is assuming a bigger motor grinds finer. Particle size is set by the shredder ring and impellers, so a half horsepower unit and a three quarter unit leave similar particles, and the larger one simply reaches speed sooner and clears a jam with less drama. Pay for the horsepower only if your cooking really generates dense scraps every night.

Many disposers ship without a cord and need a separate cord kit and a nearby outlet or hardwiring. The Badger 5 and both Moen units include a pre-installed cord, which saves a trip to the store. Check the listing for the cord, because a bare unit can cost extra time and money. Cord kits are cheap, but they add a wiring step that some owners should not do alone. If your outlet sits under the sink, a plug-in unit like the Badger 5 or the Moen PRO is the cleaner job, and it lets you unplug the unit before working on a jam, which is the safest habit with any disposal.

The mount decides how easily you can swap a unit. The Badger 5 uses a twist-on, twist-off Lift and Latch quick lock, and the Moen units claim to fit most existing assemblies, including other brands. If your sink flange is old, match the mount before buying. If you rent or expect to move, the quick lock style is worth the preference because it leaves the sink flange untouched. Measure the flange diameter and check the ring type before ordering, and keep the old mounting hardware until the new unit has run for a week without a drip.

Disposers add solids to a septic tank, which means more frequent pumping. The Badger line is listed as septic compatible. If you have a septic system, check the tank size and local rules before buying. Also check cabinet clearance, since a larger unit may collide with a trap. Septic owners should treat a disposal as extra load on the tank. Pumping intervals shorten, and a tank near capacity may not tolerate it at all. Ask your septic service about tank size, and avoid feeding fats, starchy pasta and large amounts of coffee grounds, which build up as sludge.

At this price, sound insulation is minimal. Premium units use jacketed shells and anti-vibration mounts, and those cut noise more than any horsepower figure. Expect a noisy motor and use a sink baffle to reduce splatter and sound. The cheapest way to cut noise is behavior, not hardware. Run plenty of cold water, feed scraps gradually instead of dumping a plate in one go, and fit the sink baffle properly, because a missing or loose baffle lets noise and splash escape into the kitchen.

Every disposer should have a hex socket on the bottom for freeing a jam by hand and a reset button. Fibrous waste, bones and grease cause most jams, so feed small portions with cold water running. Learn the jam routine the day you install it. Switch the unit off, unplug it, insert the hex key in the socket under the unit, rock the flywheel back and forth, then press the reset button on the housing. Never put a hand inside the chamber, even when the unit is unplugged.

specDecoder.meaning: The motor size, usually 1/3 to 1 HP. It affects speed and jam resistance. Treat it as a rough guide, because manufacturers measure it differently and a larger motor is not always better for a single person.
specDecoder.watchFor: The GE 1/3 HP is the lightest, with the Badger and Moen at 1/2 HP.

specDecoder.meaning: Flywheel speed. Higher RPM can mean finer particles. Units at higher speed tend to run louder, so a quiet unit may use a slower flywheel and rely on its insulation for noise control.
specDecoder.watchFor: The GE and Moen units list about 2,600 RPM for half horsepower and 2,300 for the third.

specDecoder.meaning: How the unit attaches to the sink flange. A mount that matches your existing ring saves a plumbing visit and avoids new flange parts.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Badger uses Lift and Latch, the Moen Fast Track.

specDecoder.meaning: Whether a power cord ships with the unit. Without a cord you must hardwire the unit, which requires a junction box and a switch that meets your local code.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Badger 5 and Moen units include one.

specDecoder.meaning: Whether the maker lists the unit as safe for septic systems. Septic safe means the unit does not harm the tank bacteria, not that it adds nothing to the solids load.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Badger is listed as septic compatible.

howToChoose.subheading: Quick Lock Mount vs Standard Flange

cards.label: Quick lock
cards.text: The Badger 5's Lift and Latch lets you twist the unit on and off the mounting ring, which saves time at replacement.

cards.label: Standard or adaptable
cards.text: The Moen Fast Track and GE kits fit many assemblies but may need more work if your flange is unusual.

howToChoose.note: Choose quick lock if you already have a compatible ring.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A septic compatible listing, modest use and a tank sized for the extra solids. Plan more frequent pumping.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Badger 5 is listed as septic compatible; check the others with the maker before buying.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You grind scraps daily or want less noise. Higher tiers add insulation and stronger motors.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cook lightly. The GE 1/3 HP does the job for the least.

maintenance.why: Cold water solidifies grease and carries particles through the trap. Fats left in the drain line harden and form clogs, so keep the water running for about fifteen seconds after the grinding stops.

maintenance.task: Clean with ice and citrus peel
maintenance.why: Ice knocks residue off the chamber and citrus freshens it. Never use bleach or drain chemicals. Grinding ice and a few citrus peels takes away odors without chemicals that attack the seals, so use it as a routine, not a rescue.

maintenance.task: Check the hex socket and reset
maintenance.why: Knowing where they sit saves time during a jam. A new reset button that has been pressed several times without success usually means a stuck flywheel or a motor fault.
Leaks from the drain connection are common and damage cabinets. Look for drips at the slip joints and the dishwasher hose, because a slow leak rots the cabinet floor long before you notice a puddle.
A damp cabinet can degrade cord insulation. Replace the cord if the jacket is hard, cracked or discolored near the plug.

faq.a: For most households, yes. A half horsepower motor handles plates, peels and soft scraps. If you grind daily or cook heavily, a larger motor gives more headroom.

faq.q: Do these include a power cord?
faq.a: The Badger 5 and Moen units list a cord. Others may need a cord kit, so check the listing.
Often yes. A DIY install takes an hour or two with basic tools. If wiring is needed, hire an electrician.

faq.q: What should I never put in a disposal?
faq.a: Grease, bones, fibrous vegetables, coffee grounds in bulk, pasta and rice in volume.
Budget models are loud because insulation is minimal. Use cold water and a sink baffle to reduce noise.

faq.q: Are they safe for septic tanks?
faq.a: The Badger is listed as septic compatible. Disposers add solids, so tanks need adequate size and more frequent pumping.
